{{Short description|Framework for mathematics education}}

In [[mathematics education]], '''APOS Theory''' is a framework of how mathematical concepts are learned. APOS Theory was developed by Ed Dubinsky and others and is based on [[Jean Piaget]]'s notion of [[reflective abstraction]]. APOS stands for Actions, Processes, Objects, Schemas, the four main mental structures involved in the theory. APOS Theory takes a [[Constructivism (philosophy of education)|constructivist]] view towards mathematical learning. Implementations of APOS Theory in classrooms typically use the '''ACE Teaching Cycle''', a pedagogical strategy with three chronological components: activities, classroom discussion, and exercises. Implementations also often use mathematical [[programming language]]s, most commonly [[ISETL]].

== Mental structures and mechanisms ==

APOS Theory emphasizes four [[mental structure]]s: Actions, Processes, Objects, and Schemas and its [[mental mechanism]]s: Interiorization, Encapsulation, Coordination, Reversal, among others.

# ''Actions'' are specific manipulations or transformations done to already understood [[mathematical object]]s.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=19}} Actions are ''external'', meaning that each step of the transformation needs to be performed explicitly and guided by external instructions.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=19}} For example, someone who can only think about [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] by substituting a number into an expression has an action understanding of functions.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=19}}
# ''Processes'' are actions that have been fully internalized. Someone who has internalized an action into a process can do the action without external instruction, can skip steps, and can imagine performing the process in the abstract without specific inputs being present.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=21}} The shift from an action understanding to a process understanding is called ''interiorization''.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=20}} For example, someone with a process understanding of a function is able to think about a function as taking in unspecified inputs and applying a transformation to them to produce an output, and someone who has a process understanding of an [[N-tuple|{{math|''n''}}-tuple]] is able to mentally consider the concept of an {{math|''n''}}-tuple for unspecified {{math|''n''}}.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=21}} 
# ''Objects'' are cognitive objects coming from the ability to conceptualize the totality of a process and understanding how to put additional structure on that totality.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=21}} The shift from a process understanding to an object understanding is called ''encapsulation''.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=21}} Someone with an object understanding of functions is able to form a set of functions and define additional structure on that set, such as operations or a [[Topological space|topology]].{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=21}} Encapsulation is considered the most difficult step in APOS-based instruction.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=22}}
# ''Schemas'' are collections of actions, processes, and objects, and other schemas, and the interactions between them, and the ability to understand in what situations it applies.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|pp=24-25}} For example, for someone who understands the theory of [[vector space]]s, the mental structure of a vector space is a schema.{{sfn|Arnon|Cottrill|Dubinsky|Oktaç|2014|p=25}}

The mental structures are not necessarily gone through in a linear progression.{{sfn|Oktaç|Trigueros|Romo|2019|p=1}}
